body: What is a digital firm?
answer:
A digital firm is an organisation in which nearly all of its significant business relationships with customers, suppliers and employees are digitally enabled and mediated, and its core business processes are accomplished through digital networks spanning the entire organisation or linking multiple organisations (Laudon & Laudon).

Characteristics:
• Key corporate assets — intellectual property, core competencies, financial and human assets — are managed through digital means.
• It senses and responds to its environment far more rapidly than traditional firms.
• "Time shifting" (business conducted continuously, 24/7) and "space shifting" (work takes place anywhere, globally).
Examples: Amazon, Google, Uber, Jumia.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Core definition: significant relationships (customers, suppliers, employees) digitally enabled — 1 mark.
• Core business processes run through digital networks — 1 mark.
• A further characteristic (digital asset management, rapid response, time/space shifting) or a valid example — 1 mark.
hint: Think of a business whose key relationships and processes run through digital networks.

body: Your manager is eager to know if information systems help businesses. Identify and explain any three usefulness of information systems to businesses.
answer:
Any three of:

1. Operational excellence/efficiency — IS automate and streamline processes (inventory, payroll, order processing), reducing costs and errors and increasing productivity. E.g. Walmart's RetailLink supply-chain system.

2. Improved decision-making — managers get accurate, real-time information through MIS, DSS, dashboards and analytics instead of guesswork, e.g. sales trends to plan stock.

3. Competitive advantage — IS enable lower costs, differentiated products and services, or a focus on niches, helping firms outperform rivals.

4. Customer and supplier intimacy — CRM and SCM systems help firms know customers, personalise service and coordinate suppliers, building loyalty and reducing costs.

5. New products, services and business models — e.g. mobile money, e-commerce, streaming.

6. Survival / compliance — IS help meet regulatory and reporting requirements (e.g. tax, banking regulations).

7. Communication and collaboration — email, intranets and collaboration tools connect staff across locations.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Three valid uses of information systems, each identified (1 mark) and explained (1 mark).
hint: Think of what IS changes in daily operations, in decision-making and in competing with rivals.

body: Business firms invest heavily in information systems to achieve six strategic business objectives. Identify and discuss any three of the strategic business objectives.
answer:
The six objectives (Laudon & Laudon) — any three discussed:

1. Operational excellence — using IS to improve efficiency and productivity of operations and lower costs (e.g. automated inventory replenishment).
2. New products, services and business models — IS enable entirely new offerings and ways of making money (e.g. Apple's iTunes/App Store, mobile money).
3. Customer and supplier intimacy — knowing and serving customers well builds loyalty and revenue; close supplier links lower costs (CRM, SCM).
4. Improved decision-making — accurate, real-time data lets managers make better decisions instead of relying on forecasts, guesses or luck.
5. Competitive advantage — achieving the above lets a firm charge less for better products, respond faster and outperform competitors (e.g. Toyota, Dell).
6. Survival — some IS investments are necessities of doing business: matching competitors (e.g. ATMs in banking) or meeting government regulations and reporting requirements.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Three of the six named objectives (1 mark each) with a discussion/example of each (1 mark each). Objectives outside Laudon's six earn credit only if clearly equivalent.
hint: Laudon's six: operational excellence; new products, services and business models; customer and supplier intimacy; improved decision-making; competitive advantage; survival.

body: What is the technical definition of an organization?
answer:
Technically (microeconomic definition), an organization is a stable, formal social structure that takes resources (capital and labour — inputs) from the environment and processes them to produce outputs (products and services) that are consumed by the environment.

It is formal (has rules and procedures), a legal entity, and a social structure — a collection of social elements, like a machine with inputs, processing and outputs.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Stable, formal social structure — 1 mark.
• Takes resources from the environment and processes them into outputs — 1 mark.
hint: Microeconomic view: inputs from the environment → processing → outputs back to it.

body: Distinguish between organizational politics and organizational culture.
answer:
Organizational politics:
• Arises because people in an organisation occupy different positions with different specialties, concerns and perspectives, and naturally hold divergent viewpoints about how resources, rewards and punishments should be distributed.
• These differences lead to political struggle, competition and conflict for power and resources.
• Relevance to IS: information systems change who controls information and resources, so new systems often meet political resistance — a major reason IS projects fail.

Organizational culture:
• The fundamental set of assumptions, values and ways of doing things that has been accepted by most members of the organisation (e.g. "the customer comes first", "we are a technology leader").
• It shapes behaviour, decisions, products and processes; usually stable and taken for granted.
• Relevance to IS: culture can be a unifying force that supports technology, but it can also restrain change when new systems challenge existing assumptions.

Key distinction: politics is about conflict and competition among divergent interests; culture is about shared, unifying assumptions and values.
explanation:
Marking guide (5 marks):
• Organizational politics correctly explained (divergent interests, competition for resources/power, conflict) — 2 marks.
• Organizational culture correctly explained (shared assumptions, values, norms) — 2 marks.
• Clear contrast and/or link to information systems (resistance to change) — 1 mark.
hint: One is about competing interests and power; the other is about shared assumptions and values.

body: Interaction between information technology and organisations is influenced by many mediating factors. State and discuss any four of the mediating factors.
answer:
The mediating factors (Laudon & Laudon) — any four discussed:

1. Environment — external conditions (economy, regulation, competition, technology change, customers) influence which systems an organisation needs and adopts; IT also helps the organisation monitor and respond to its environment.

2. Organizational structure — whether the firm is an entrepreneurial structure, machine bureaucracy, divisionalized bureaucracy, professional bureaucracy or adhocracy shapes the kinds of systems built and how they are used.

3. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) — precise rules and routines developed to cope with expected situations; new systems that change SOPs face resistance and require costly retraining.

4. Business processes — the way work is organised, coordinated and focused; IT can automate or redesign them, but existing processes constrain how technology is applied.

5. Organizational politics — divergent interests compete for resources; systems that shift power meet political resistance.

6. Organizational culture — shared assumptions and values may support or block new technology.

7. Management decisions — managers' choices about which technology to adopt, how to fund and implement it, and how to change the organisation determine the outcome.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• Four valid mediating factors: each named (0.5 marks) and discussed in relation to how it shapes the IT–organisation interaction (1.5 marks).
hint: Laudon lists: environment, structure, standard operating procedures, business processes, politics, culture, management decisions.

body: Differentiate between a telephone network and a computer network.
answer:
Telephone network:
• Historically built to carry voice (analog signals) between telephones.
• Uses circuit switching: a dedicated end-to-end circuit is set up for the whole call.
• Managed by telecom carriers using centralised exchanges; billed per call/minute.

Computer network:
• Built to carry digital data between computers and devices so they can share resources (files, printers, Internet access, applications).
• Uses packet switching: data is broken into packets that travel independently over shared links (e.g. TCP/IP).
• Can be owned by the organisation (LAN/WAN), with servers, switches and routers.

Today the two are converging: voice is carried as data (VoIP) over packet-switched networks.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Telephone network described (voice, circuit-switched) — 1 mark.
• Computer network described (data, resource sharing, packet-switched) — 1 mark.
• Clear contrast or note on convergence/VoIP — 1 mark.
hint: Compare what each was built to carry and how it switches traffic.

body: Differentiate between a server and a hub.
answer:
Server:
• A computer (hardware and software) on a network that provides services and resources to client computers — e.g. file, web, email, database, print or application services.
• Has processing power, storage and an operating system; responds to client requests.

Hub:
• A very simple network connecting device (layer 1) that links several computers in a LAN.
• It receives data on one port and broadcasts it to all other ports, without examining addresses — so it causes collisions and wastes bandwidth. (Largely replaced by switches, which send data only to the intended port.)

Difference: a server provides services; a hub merely connects devices and repeats signals, with no intelligence or services of its own.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Server correctly described — 1 mark.
• Hub correctly described (connects devices, broadcasts to all ports) — 1 mark.
• Clear contrast — 1 mark.
hint: One is a computer that provides services; the other is a simple box that connects cables.

body: Differentiate between packet switching and circuit switching.
answer:
Circuit switching:
• A dedicated, end-to-end physical path is established between sender and receiver before communication starts and is held for the whole session, whether or not data is flowing (traditional telephone calls).
• Guaranteed bandwidth and constant delay, but wasteful — capacity sits idle during silences — and setup takes time.

Packet switching:
• Messages are broken into small packets, each with addressing information, that travel independently over shared network paths (possibly by different routes) and are reassembled at the destination (the Internet, TCP/IP).
• Makes efficient use of capacity, robust (packets reroute around failures) and cheaper, but delay can vary and packets may arrive out of order.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Circuit switching explained (dedicated path for the session) — 1 mark.
• Packet switching explained (packets routed independently over shared links, reassembled) — 1 mark.
• A valid contrast (efficiency, reliability, cost, delay) — 1 mark.
hint: Dedicated path for the whole conversation vs small chunks sharing the road.

body: Write down and discuss the three types of networks.
answer:
1. Local Area Network (LAN) — connects computers and devices within a limited area such as an office, building or campus (up to about 500 m–a few km). Usually owned by one organisation; high speed (Ethernet, Wi-Fi), low cost, low error rate. E.g. a university computer lab.

2. Metropolitan Area Network (MAN) — spans a city or metropolitan area, linking several LANs (e.g. a bank's branches across Accra or a city-wide fibre network). Larger than a LAN, smaller than a WAN, often run by a service provider.

3. Wide Area Network (WAN) — covers large geographical distances — regions, countries or the whole world — linking LANs and MANs using leased lines, satellite, fibre or public networks. Typically slower and costlier per unit than LANs. The Internet is the largest WAN.

(Also acceptable if discussed: Campus Area Network (CAN) or Personal Area Network (PAN); or a classification by architecture: peer-to-peer vs client/server.)
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Three network types, each named (0.5 marks) and discussed with scope/characteristics/example (1.5 marks). LAN, MAN and WAN expected; CAN/PAN or peer-to-peer vs client/server accepted if well discussed.
hint: Classify by geographic area: local, metropolitan, wide.

body: What is a digital good? Give two examples.
answer:
A digital good is a product that can be produced, stored, delivered and sold over a digital network — it exists as data rather than a physical object. Its cost of producing the first copy is high, but the marginal cost of producing and distributing another copy is almost zero; it is easy to copy and has low inventory and delivery costs.

Examples: music tracks (Spotify, Apple Music), e-books, software and apps, films and videos (Netflix), online newspapers, video games, digital photos/stock images, online courses.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Definition: goods deliverable over a digital network (with characteristics such as near-zero marginal cost) — 1 mark.
• Two valid examples — 1 mark each.
hint: Goods that can be delivered over a network. What is their marginal cost of producing one more copy?

body: Discuss any three E-commerce business models.
answer:
Any three of:

1. E-tailer (online retail store) — sells physical products directly to customers or individual businesses; revenue from sales. E.g. Amazon, Jumia.
2. Transaction broker — saves users money and time by processing online sales transactions, earning a fee each time, e.g. online travel agents (Expedia, Booking.com), online brokerage.
3. Market creator — provides a digital environment where buyers and sellers meet, search for and display products, and set prices; earns fees/commissions. E.g. eBay, Tonaton, Uber.
4. Content provider — creates revenue by providing digital content (news, music, video, photos) over the web; subscriptions, pay-per-download or ads. E.g. Netflix, Spotify.
5. Community provider (social network) — an online meeting place where people with similar interests communicate; revenue from ads and subscriptions. E.g. Facebook, LinkedIn.
6. Portal — an initial point of entry to the web with specialised content and services; advertising revenue. E.g. Yahoo, MSN.
7. Service provider — provides Web 2.0 applications such as photo sharing, video sharing and storage; fees, subscriptions, ads. E.g. Google Docs, Dropbox.

(Also accept: B2C, B2B, C2C, M-commerce, freemium, subscription, advertising models, if properly discussed.)
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Three valid e-commerce business models, each named (0.5 marks) and discussed with how it creates value/earns revenue and an example (1.5 marks).
hint: Laudon's models: e-tailer, transaction broker, market creator, content provider, community provider, portal, service provider. (B2C/B2B/C2C are e-commerce types, which may also be accepted.)

body: Explain the following feature of E-Commerce technology: Ubiquity
answer: Ubiquity means e-commerce technology is available everywhere and at all times — at work, at home, on the move via mobile devices, 24/7. The marketplace is extended beyond traditional physical boundaries and removed from a temporal and geographic location, creating a "marketspace". For consumers this reduces transaction costs (the time, effort and cost of travelling to a market to shop).
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Available anywhere, anytime — 1 mark.
• Consequence: marketspace beyond physical/temporal limits, reduced shopping/transaction costs — 1 mark.
hint: Where and when can you shop online?

body: Explain the following feature of E-Commerce technology: Customization
answer: Customization means changing the delivered product or service based on a user's preferences or prior behaviour. E-commerce technology makes it possible to tailor products, services and content to each individual at low cost, e.g. configuring a laptop on Dell's site, a personalised news feed, or custom-printed products. (It is closely related to personalization, which targets marketing messages to individuals.)
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Changing the product/service according to user preferences or behaviour — 1 mark.
• Example or note on low cost/personalization — 1 mark.
hint: Can the product itself change for each buyer?

body: Explain the following feature of E-Commerce technology: Information density
answer:
Information density is the total amount and quality of information available to all market participants — consumers and merchants. E-commerce greatly increases it while lowering the costs of collecting, storing, processing and communicating information.

Effects: consumers gain price and cost transparency (they can easily compare prices and learn true costs); merchants learn much more about consumers, enabling price discrimination and market segmentation.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Increase in the amount/quality of information available to buyers and sellers at lower cost — 1 mark.
• Effect: price/cost transparency, price discrimination or segmentation — 1 mark.
hint: Think about the amount and quality of information available to buyers and sellers.

body: Distinguish between security and controls as used in system vulnerability and abuse.
answer:
Security refers to the policies, procedures and technical measures used to prevent unauthorized access, alteration, theft or physical damage to information systems.

Controls are the methods, policies and organizational procedures that ensure the safety of the organization's assets, the accuracy and reliability of its records, and operational adherence to management standards.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Security defined (policies, procedures, technical measures preventing unauthorized access, alteration, theft, damage) — 1 mark.
• Controls defined (methods, policies, procedures ensuring asset safety, record accuracy/reliability, adherence to standards) — 1 mark.
hint: One is about policies and measures to prevent harm; the other is about methods ensuring safety, accuracy and adherence.

body: Distinguish between a virus and spyware.
answer:
Computer virus:
• A rogue software program that attaches itself to other software programs or data files in order to be executed, usually without the user's knowledge or permission.
• It replicates and spreads when infected files are shared or run.
• Its payload may be harmless (displaying messages) or destructive — corrupting or deleting files, reformatting disks, disrupting systems.

Spyware:
• Software that installs itself covertly on computers (often bundled with free downloads) to monitor the user's activity.
• It gathers information such as web-surfing habits, keystrokes (key loggers), passwords and personal data, and sends it to third parties, often for advertising or identity theft.
• It usually does not replicate; its aim is surveillance and data theft rather than damage, though it slows systems and breaches privacy.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Virus explained (attaches to programs/files, replicates, payload/damage) — 2 marks.
• Spyware explained (covertly installed, monitors activity, steals/sends information) — 2 marks.
hint: One spreads by attaching to other programs and does damage; the other quietly watches what you do.

body: What is the major difference between hackers and crackers in terms of system intrusion, system damage and cyber vandalism?
answer:
• A hacker is an individual who intends to gain unauthorized access to a computer system, often out of curiosity, for the challenge, or to discover weaknesses — not necessarily to cause harm.
• A cracker is a hacker with criminal intent: one who breaks into systems to steal, damage, destroy or disrupt.

System intrusion: both gain unauthorized access, but crackers do so with malicious purpose.
System damage and cyber vandalism: crackers intentionally disrupt, deface or destroy websites and corporate information systems; hackers (in the original sense) aim to explore rather than damage.

(In popular usage the terms are often used interchangeably, and "hacker" is often used for both.)
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Hacker: unauthorized access, often for curiosity/challenge — 1 mark.
• Cracker: hacker with criminal/malicious intent — 1 mark.
• Applied to intrusion, system damage and cyber vandalism — 1 mark.
hint: Both break in; the difference is intent.

body: List and explain any three important tools and technologies for safeguarding information systems.
answer:
Any three of:

1. Identity management and authentication — passwords, tokens, smart cards and biometrics verify that users are who they claim to be; access is granted only to authorized users.
2. Firewalls — hardware/software that controls the flow of incoming and outgoing network traffic according to security rules, blocking unauthorized access.
3. Intrusion detection systems (IDS) — monitor networks for suspicious activity and alert administrators in real time.
4. Antivirus and anti-malware software — detect and remove viruses, worms, spyware and other malware.
5. Encryption and public key infrastructure (PKI) — encode data so only authorized parties can read it; digital certificates verify identities (SSL/TLS).
6. Unified threat management (UTM) — combines firewall, IDS, antivirus, content filtering in one appliance.
7. Ensuring system availability — fault-tolerant systems, backups, disaster recovery and business continuity planning.
8. Securing wireless networks — WPA2/WPA3 encryption.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Three valid tools/technologies, each named and briefly explained — 1 mark each.
hint: Think of controlling who gets in, stopping bad traffic, and protecting data even if it's stolen.

body: State any three factors that contribute to the vulnerabilities of information systems.
answer:
Any three of:
1. Network accessibility — networks (especially the Internet) are open and accessible from anywhere, so data can be intercepted or systems attacked remotely.
2. Hardware problems — breakdowns, configuration errors, damage from improper use.
3. Software problems — programming errors (bugs), poor design, unpatched vulnerabilities, installation errors and unauthorized changes.
4. Malicious software and attacks — viruses, worms, hacking, denial-of-service.
5. Human factors — employee errors, weak passwords, social engineering, insider threats.
6. Disasters — power failures, floods, fires and other natural disasters.
7. Use of networks and computers outside the firm's control — e.g. outsourcing partners, cloud services, mobile devices and wireless networks that are easily penetrated.
8. Loss or theft of portable devices.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Three valid factors — 1 mark each (stated with a brief explanation).
hint: Think technical, organisational and environmental: networks, software, people, disasters.
